questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying the renal action of furosemide. The diagram below shows the principal apical and basolateral transporters of the thick ascending limb of Henle. Loop diuretics inhibit a single apical transporter that mediates electroneutral cotransport of three ions in stoichiometry 1:1:2. Which of the following transporters is the target of loop diuretics?
questions.diagram:
Thick ascending limb (TAL) — site of loop diuretic action
Apical: NKCC2 (Na+ + K+ + 2Cl− → cell) ← BLOCKED by furosemide / bumetanide / torsemide / ethacrynic acid
Apical: ROMK recycles K+ to lumen → lumen-positive voltage
Basolateral: Na+/K+-ATPase, ClC-Kb (Cl− out)
Lumen-positive voltage drives paracellular Mg2+ + Ca2+ reabsorption (claudin-16/19)
Water IMPERMEABLE → 'diluting segment' AND generator of medullary osmotic gradient
choices: NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger of the proximal tubule)
NCC (Na+-Cl− cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule)
NKCC2 (Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter of the thick ascending limb)
ENaC (epithelial Na+ channel of collecting duct principal cells)
Apical Na+/K+-ATPase
explanations: Incorrect. NHE3 is the proximal tubule's apical Na+/H+ exchanger, blocked by acetazolamide-class effects in some species; not the loop diuretic target.
Incorrect. NCC is the apical Na+-Cl− cotransporter of the early distal convoluted tubule, blocked by thiazide diuretics.

Correct. Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, and the non-sulfa drug ethacrynic acid) inhibit NKCC2 in the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb. Blockade of NKCC2 abolishes the active reabsorption of Na+, K+, and 2Cl−; abolishes the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage that drives paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption; impairs both urinary concentration and dilution; and produces a brisk natriuresis. Loop diuretics are the most efficacious diuretic class.
Incorrect. ENaC is the principal cell apical Na+ channel, blocked by amiloride and triamterene.
Incorrect. Na+/K+-ATPase is basolateral throughout the nephron and is not the apical loop diuretic target.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with heart failure is taking oral furosemide. To produce its natriuretic effect, furosemide must reach the LUMINAL side of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. Given that furosemide is approximately 95% bound to plasma albumin (and therefore poorly filtered), how does it reach this luminal site of action?
choices: Free filtration at the glomerulus, since plasma binding does not affect filtration
Active secretion via OAT1/OAT3 in the proximal tubule
Passive diffusion across the glomerular basement membrane
Pinocytosis by proximal tubular cells
Active reabsorption from peritubular capillaries directly into the TAL lumen
explanations: Incorrect. The high protein binding (~95%) means furosemide is poorly filtered; filtration alone cannot deliver therapeutic concentrations to the TAL.

Correct. Loop diuretics (and thiazides, acetazolamide) are weak organic acids that are actively secreted into the proximal tubular lumen by basolateral organic anion transporters (OAT1, OAT3) — the same family that handles uric acid, β-lactams, and many drugs. Apical multidrug-resistance proteins then move drug into the lumen. Tubular fluid concentrations exceed plasma concentrations, allowing the drug to act at NKCC2. Competing organic anions (e.g., uremic toxins in CKD, NSAIDs, probenecid) reduce loop diuretic delivery to the lumen — explaining diminished diuretic effect in renal failure.
Incorrect. The GBM has fenestrated barriers that depend on size and charge; bound drug is not transported by passive GBM diffusion.
Incorrect. Pinocytosis is not the principal route of loop diuretic delivery to the tubule.
Incorrect. There is no direct active reabsorption pathway delivering furosemide from peritubular capillaries to the TAL lumen.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on chronic furosemide for heart failure cannot concentrate his urine even when his fluid intake is restricted. Maximum urine osmolality is approximately 350 mOsm/kg (versus an expected ~1200 mOsm/kg in his age group). Which of the following best explains this concentrating defect?
choices: Reduced posterior pituitary ADH secretion induced by furosemide
Direct destruction of AQP2 channels in collecting duct principal cells
Volume contraction triggering compensatory water loss
Direct toxicity of furosemide to collecting duct epithelium
Inhibition of NKCC2 abolishes the medullary osmotic gradient
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly suppress ADH secretion.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not destroy AQP2 channels; the defect is in the medullary gradient that drives water reabsorption, not in the channel.
Incorrect. Volume contraction does not by itself impair concentrating ability; if anything, it activates ADH.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not produce direct collecting duct toxicity at therapeutic doses.

Correct. The TAL is essential to countercurrent multiplication: it actively transports NaCl from tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium, generating the medullary osmotic gradient. NKCC2 inhibition abolishes this transport, so the gradient runs down. Without the gradient, even fully active ADH-driven AQP2 insertion cannot concentrate urine because there is no osmotic 'engine' to drive water reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct. Maximum urine osmolality therefore approaches plasma osmolality (~290–350 mOsm/kg).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on chronic furosemide undergoes a water-loading test. His maximum urinary dilution is impaired (urine osmolality cannot fall below ~200 mOsm/kg, versus the expected ~50 in healthy individuals). Which of the following best explains this diluting defect?
choices: Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the diluting segment of the nephron
Loop diuretics directly increase ADH release
Loop diuretics directly increase apical AQP2 insertion in the collecting duct
Loop diuretics block ENaC in the collecting duct
Loop diuretics activate carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
explanations: Correct. The TAL plays a unique role: it is water-impermeable but actively reabsorbs NaCl, delivering tubular fluid to the DCT and collecting duct that is HYPOTONIC to plasma. This 'diluting segment' function allows the kidney to excrete dilute urine when free water needs to be lost (low ADH state). Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the TAL, so the fluid leaving is closer to ISOTONIC; even with ADH suppressed, urinary dilution is limited. The loss of both concentrating AND diluting ability — leaving only isosthenuric urine — is a hallmark of loop diuretic action.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly stimulate ADH release.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not increase AQP2 insertion; the impaired dilution is upstream of the collecting duct.
Incorrect. ENaC blockade is the mechanism of K+-sparing diuretics, not loop diuretics.
Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase activation is not a feature of loop diuretic action.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has been taking high-dose furosemide for refractory heart failure. Her serum magnesium is 1.3 mg/dL (low) and her 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is elevated. Which of the following best explains the loss of magnesium and calcium in this patient?
choices: Direct inhibition of an apical Mg2+ pump in the TAL
Direct inhibition of an apical Ca2+ pump in the TAL
Hypoalbuminemia reducing protein-bound Mg2+ and Ca2+
NKCC2 inhibition eliminates the lumen-positive voltage driving paracellular Mg2+/Ca2+
Loop diuretics chemically chelate Mg2+ and Ca2+ in plasma
explanations: Incorrect. There is no apical Mg2+ pump in the TAL; Mg2+ is reabsorbed paracellularly down its electrochemical gradient.
Incorrect. There is no apical Ca2+ pump in the TAL; Ca2+ is reabsorbed paracellularly via claudin-16/19.
Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia would lower TOTAL Mg2+/Ca2+ measurements but not the ionized fraction; this is not the principal mechanism here.

Correct. NKCC2 takes Na+, K+, and 2Cl− into the TAL cell. K+ then recycles back into the lumen through apical ROMK, generating the lumen-POSITIVE transepithelial voltage. This voltage drives paracellular reabsorption of Mg2+ and Ca2+ via claudin-16/19. Loop diuretics block NKCC2 → no K+ entry → no ROMK recycling → no lumen-positive voltage → reduced paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption → urinary wasting. Hypomagnesemia and hypercalciuria are characteristic adverse effects (the latter is exploited therapeutically in hypercalcemia).
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not chemically chelate Mg2+ or Ca2+.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with HFrEF has variable response to oral furosemide from day to day, despite taking the same dose. His clinician considers switching to bumetanide or torsemide. Which of the following best characterizes the oral pharmacokinetics that may explain his variable response?
choices: Oral furosemide has near-complete and reliable bioavailability of >95%
Oral furosemide has variable bioavailability (~50%, range 10–90%)
Oral furosemide undergoes 100% hepatic first-pass metabolism
Oral furosemide is not absorbed from the GI tract at all
Oral furosemide must be given with food to be absorbed
explanations: Incorrect. Furosemide's oral bioavailability is variable and incomplete — far from 95%.

Correct. Furosemide oral bioavailability averages ~50% but ranges widely (10–90%) between and within patients, due to inconsistent GI absorption (poor solubility at acidic pH) and gastric emptying. Bumetanide and torsemide both have more reliable bioavailability (~80–100%). When patients on stable oral furosemide doses respond inconsistently, switching to bumetanide or torsemide can give more predictable absorption — and is sometimes preferred in HF management.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics undergo modest hepatic metabolism but not 100% first-pass.
Incorrect. Furosemide is absorbed orally; the issue is variability, not absence.
Incorrect. Food may slow absorption modestly but is not required for absorption.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with chronic heart failure is being switched from furosemide 80 mg PO BID to bumetanide for more reliable bioavailability. Which of the following is the most appropriate equipotent oral dose of bumetanide?
choices: Bumetanide 80 mg PO BID
Bumetanide 40 mg PO BID
Bumetanide 1 mg PO BID
Bumetanide 200 mg PO BID
Bumetanide 800 mg PO BID
explanations: Incorrect. This dose far exceeds equipotent dosing and would risk severe hypokalemia and ototoxicity.
Incorrect. This is much greater than the equipotent dose; bumetanide is far more potent on a mg-for-mg basis.

Correct. Equipotency: 1 mg bumetanide ≈ 10 mg torsemide ≈ 20 mg furosemide IV ≈ 40 mg furosemide PO. So furosemide 80 mg PO ≈ bumetanide 2 mg PO; furosemide 80 mg BID ≈ bumetanide 1 mg BID approximately (the question asks about equipotent dose for the daily total). Bumetanide's smaller dose units and more reliable bioavailability make it useful for some HF patients with poor response to oral furosemide.
Incorrect. Far exceeds equipotent dose.
Incorrect. Far exceeds equipotent dose.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with HFrEF is being considered for once-daily oral diuretic dosing to improve adherence. Compared with furosemide, which of the following best characterizes torsemide?
choices: Longer half-life and more reliable oral bioavailability than furosemide
Shorter half-life than furosemide
Acts at NCC in the DCT instead of NKCC2 in the TAL
Is a potassium-sparing diuretic
Is contraindicated in heart failure
explanations: Correct. Torsemide has a half-life of ~3–4 hours (vs furosemide ~1.5–2), more reliable oral bioavailability (~80%, vs furosemide ~50%), and is more often suitable for once-daily oral dosing. Some observational data and the TRANSFORM-HF trial have suggested potential outcome advantages of torsemide over furosemide in HFrEF, though randomized data remain mixed. Torsemide also has some natriuretic effect via aldosterone receptor antagonism at high doses, though NKCC2 inhibition is its primary mechanism.
Incorrect. Torsemide's half-life is LONGER, not shorter.
Incorrect. Torsemide acts at NKCC2 in the TAL, the same site as other loop diuretics.
Incorrect. Torsemide is a loop diuretic; potassium-sparing diuretics target ENaC or the mineralocorticoid receptor.
Incorrect. Torsemide is a guideline-recommended loop diuretic for HFrEF.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with acute pulmonary edema is given IV furosemide. He reports rapid relief of dyspnea within 15 minutes — well before any significant urine output has occurred. Which of the following best explains this pre-diuretic clinical benefit?
choices: Direct inhibition of ENaC in collecting duct principal cells
Direct decrease in cardiac output by furosemide
Direct antagonism of vasopressin receptors
IV venodilator effect mediated by prostaglandin release
Direct β1-adrenergic activation
explanations: Incorrect. ENaC inhibition is the mechanism of K+-sparing diuretics and is not relevant to the rapid IV furosemide effect.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly reduce cardiac output; they reduce preload via venodilation and diuresis.
Incorrect. Furosemide does not antagonize vasopressin receptors; tolvaptan does.

Correct. IV loop diuretics produce a venodilator effect within minutes, likely via prostaglandin release, that reduces cardiac preload and pulmonary capillary pressure. This 'prediuretic' hemodynamic improvement explains why dyspnea often improves rapidly after IV furosemide, BEFORE significant urine output. Note: NSAIDs (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) blunt this effect.
Incorrect. Furosemide does not have direct β1-adrenergic activity.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with severe hypercalcemia (Ca 14.5 mg/dL), nausea, and confusion. After aggressive isotonic saline volume repletion, IV furosemide is added once she is volume-replete. Compared with no diuretic, which row best characterizes the effect of the loop diuretic on calcium handling in this patient?
choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Correct. Loop diuretics inhibit NKCC2, abolishing the lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Ca2+ reabsorption in the TAL — INCREASING urinary Ca2+ excretion and lowering serum Ca2+. This calciuric effect is exploited in hypercalcemia management AFTER volume repletion (using furosemide before adequate volume can WORSEN hypercalcemia by aggravating volume depletion and reducing GFR). Modern guidelines emphasize saline alone as primary, with loop diuretic added only when volume overload is a concern; bisphosphonates and calcitonin are the principal pharmacologic agents.
Incorrect. Decreased urinary Ca with increased serum Ca describes THIAZIDE diuretics — and thiazides are CONTRAINDICATED in hypercalcemia because they raise serum Ca2+.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics produce hypercalciuria (↑ urine Ca2+), not hypocalciuria.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics act on NKCC2; this row's pattern misses the mechanism.
Incorrect. The point of using a loop diuretic in hypercalcemia is to LOWER serum Ca2+; this option's serum Ca rising is the opposite of the desired effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with advanced cirrhosis and tense ascites is being started on diuretic therapy. Which of the following is the preferred initial diuretic regimen for cirrhotic ascites?
choices: Furosemide alone, titrated for goal weight loss
Spironolactone alone at low doses
Hydrochlorothiazide alone
ACE inhibitor alone
Combined spironolactone + furosemide in 100:40 ratio
explanations: Incorrect. Furosemide alone in cirrhosis often produces hypokalemia and does not address the aldosterone-driven Na+ retention; spironolactone is preferred as the FIRST agent.
Incorrect. Spironolactone alone is a reasonable first-line option in mild ascites, but combination is more effective for moderate-to-severe ascites.
Incorrect. Thiazides have minimal natriuretic effect at the renal function levels typically seen in advanced cirrhosis and are not recommended.
Incorrect. ACE inhibitors lower renal perfusion in cirrhotic patients with low effective arterial volume, risking AKI; they are not standard ascites therapy.

Correct. Cirrhotic ascites results from splanchnic vasodilation reducing effective arterial volume, with reflex RAAS, sympathetic, and ADH activation driving Na+ and water retention. Spironolactone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism) directly addresses the aldosterone excess; furosemide adds tubular natriuresis. The fixed 100:40 ratio (spiro:furosemide) maintains K+ balance — losses from one are matched by gains from the other. Sodium restriction (≤2 g/day) is essential. Refractory ascites may require large-volume paracentesis with albumin or TIPS.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man on chronic furosemide develops K+ 2.8 mEq/L. Beyond the increased distal Na+ delivery to the collecting duct (a recognized mechanism), which of the following BEST describes another major contributor to renal K+ wasting in patients on chronic loop diuretic therapy?
choices: Direct activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase by furosemide at principal cells
Volume contraction activates RAAS with aldosterone-driven K+ secretion
Loop diuretic blocks K+ reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Loop diuretic directly blocks ROMK in principal cells
Loop diuretic directly increases adrenal aldosterone synthesis without RAAS activation
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly activate the Na+/K+-ATPase.

Correct. Three convergent mechanisms drive renal K+ wasting on chronic loop diuretics: (1) increased distal Na+ delivery (more Na+ for ENaC reabsorption, generating a more lumen-negative voltage that drives K+ secretion via ROMK); (2) increased urine flow rate (washes K+ away from the apical membrane and activates flow-dependent BK channels); and (3) volume contraction–mediated RAAS activation (high aldosterone amplifies ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase). The same triad explains thiazide-induced hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not block K+ reabsorption in the PCT (where K+ is largely paracellular).
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly block ROMK; they act at NKCC2 in the TAL.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly stimulate adrenal aldosterone synthesis; they activate aldosterone INDIRECTLY through RAAS.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with HFrEF on chronic furosemide 80 mg twice daily presents with fatigue, palpitations, and muscle weakness. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Direct enhancement of α-intercalated cell H+ secretion by furosemide
Loss of HCO3− from vomiting that the patient has not reported
Volume contraction activates RAAS with chloride-responsive alkalosis
Decreased aldosterone secretion
Direct generation of HCO3− by furosemide
explanations: Incorrect. Furosemide does not directly enhance α-intercalated cell H+ secretion; the alkalosis is driven by RAAS activation and chloride depletion.
Incorrect. Vomiting can produce a similar alkalosis, but no GI losses are reported in this patient on chronic loop diuretic therapy.

Correct. Chronic loop diuretic therapy produces a 'classic' triad of hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The mechanism: (1) volume contraction → RAAS activation → aldosterone raises ENaC, ROMK, Na+/K+-ATPase, and α-intercalated cell H+-ATPase activity; (2) hypokalemia itself drives intracellular acidosis at α-intercalated cells, enhancing H+ secretion; (3) chloride loss creates a chloride-responsive alkalosis (the kidney cannot excrete the excess HCO3− without adequate Cl−). Concurrent hypomagnesemia removes ROMK's Mg2+-dependent inhibition, perpetuating K+ wasting. Treatment: Cl− and K+ + Mg2+ replacement; consider K+-sparing diuretic; address underlying volume contraction.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is INCREASED, not decreased, in this volume-contracted state.
Incorrect. Furosemide does not directly generate HCO3−.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with severe pulmonary edema received IV furosemide 200 mg over 2 hours and had 3 L of diuresis. His blood pressure has fallen from 165/95 to 100/65 mm Hg, and laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Acute lactic acidosis
Acute infection causing sepsis
Acute kidney injury alone
Contraction alkalosis (chloride-responsive)
Direct generation of HCO3− by furosemide
explanations: Incorrect. Lactic acidosis would produce a low (not high) HCO3− with elevated anion gap.
Incorrect. The picture is acute hemodynamic / electrolyte change after diuresis, not infection.
Incorrect. AKI alone does not directly produce metabolic alkalosis with low Cl−.

Correct. Aggressive diuresis with loop diuretics produces a 'contraction alkalosis': the urine has more Cl− (and water) than HCO3−, so the residual ECF has a higher HCO3−/Cl− ratio. The HCO3− is essentially unchanged in absolute amount but more concentrated. This is termed 'chloride-responsive' because restoring volume and Cl− with isotonic saline allows the kidney to excrete the excess HCO3− and corrects the alkalosis. The associated hypokalemia and volume contraction reactivate RAAS, which can perpetuate the alkalosis through aldosterone-driven H+ secretion. Differs from chloride-RESISTANT alkalosis (e.g., Conn syndrome) where saline does not correct the alkalosis.
Incorrect. Furosemide does not directly generate HCO3−; the alkalosis is volume-contraction driven.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on chronic furosemide develops new-onset asymptomatic hypomagnesemia (Mg2+ 1.3 mg/dL). Which of the following best describes the mechanism of furosemide-induced hypomagnesemia?
choices: Loss of TAL lumen-positive voltage driving paracellular Mg2+ reabsorption
Direct inhibition of an apical Mg2+ pump in the TAL
Loss of NCC-mediated Mg2+ reabsorption in the DCT
Increased GI Mg2+ losses driven by loop diuretic therapy
Increased Mg2+ binding to plasma proteins
explanations: Correct. Mg2+ is principally reabsorbed paracellularly in the TAL, driven by the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage generated by ROMK-mediated K+ recycling. Loop diuretics block NKCC2, abolish K+ recycling, and abolish the lumen-positive voltage — eliminating the principal Mg2+ reabsorptive driving force. Urinary Mg2+ excretion rises and serum Mg2+ falls. Hypomagnesemia is common with chronic loop use and contributes to (a) refractory hypokalemia (low intracellular Mg2+ removes its inhibition of ROMK, allowing inappropriate K+ secretion) and (b) cardiac arrhythmia risk.
Incorrect. There is no apical Mg2+ pump in the TAL; Mg2+ moves paracellularly.
Incorrect. NCC-mediated Mg2+ reabsorption is not a recognized mechanism; the DCT does have TRPM6 for active Mg2+ uptake, but this is not the principal site lost with loop diuretics.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not increase GI Mg2+ losses.
Incorrect. Mg2+ binding to plasma proteins does not change with loop diuretics.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man on chronic furosemide for HF develops acute gout in his right great toe. Serum uric acid is 9.5 mg/dL (high). Which of the following best explains the mechanism of furosemide-induced hyperuricemia?
choices: Direct stimulation of uric acid synthesis by furosemide
Volume contraction enhances proximal urate reabsorption via URAT1
Direct enhancement of xanthine oxidase activity
Direct decrease in renal blood flow lowering uric acid filtration
Massive cellular release of uric acid from injured tissue
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not directly stimulate uric acid synthesis.

Correct. Diuretic-induced hyperuricemia is principally mediated by volume contraction. The proximal tubule reabsorbs urate via URAT1, which exchanges urate for organic anions including Cl−. Volume contraction enhances proximal Na+ reabsorption (with water and urate following), reducing urinary urate excretion and raising serum urate. Hyperuricemia can precipitate acute gout. The same mechanism applies to thiazide diuretics. Management: alternate diuretic strategy if possible; treat acute gout (NSAIDs, colchicine, steroids); consider urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) for chronic management.
Incorrect. Furosemide does not enhance xanthine oxidase activity.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics do not principally lower uric acid filtration.
Incorrect. There is no tissue injury releasing uric acid in this scenario.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman in the ICU has received IV furosemide 80 mg push doses three times daily for 5 days, alongside IV tobramycin (renally adjusted) for resistant pneumonia. She now reports new bilateral hearing loss and tinnitus, and audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Direct cochlear toxicity from aminoglycoside alone (loop diuretic is not ototoxic)
Direct cochlear toxicity from furosemide alone (aminoglycosides are not ototoxic)
Acute middle-ear infection unrelated to medications
Otosclerosis presenting acutely
Synergistic ototoxicity from concurrent loop diuretic and aminoglycoside
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics ARE ototoxic (especially IV push at high doses); the synergy with aminoglycosides is the issue here.
Incorrect. Aminoglycosides ARE ototoxic; the synergy with loop diuretics drove the rapid SNHL.
Incorrect. Acute middle-ear infection produces conductive (not sensorineural) hearing loss with otoscopic abnormalities.
Incorrect. Otosclerosis is a slowly progressive conductive hearing loss, not acute SNHL after pharmacotherapy.

Correct. Loop diuretics inhibit a related cotransporter (NKCC1) in the stria vascularis of the cochlea, reducing endolymph K+ secretion that is essential for sensory hair cell function. Aminoglycosides accumulate in cochlear hair cells and cause direct toxicity. Combined, they produce SYNERGISTIC ototoxicity. Risk factors: rapid IV push, high doses, renal impairment (drug accumulation), prolonged duration. Ethacrynic acid is the most ototoxic loop diuretic. Strategies to reduce risk: slow infusion (over 10–20 min), avoid concurrent aminoglycoside if possible, use lowest effective dose, monitor renal function and drug levels.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with documented severe sulfonamide allergy (anaphylaxis) requires a loop diuretic for acute heart failure exacerbation. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice?
choices: Furosemide despite the allergy history (most patients tolerate it)
Hydrochlorothiazide (also a sulfonamide)
Ethacrynic acid (the only non-sulfonamide loop diuretic)
Acetazolamide (also a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor)
Spironolactone (a non-sulfonamide K+-sparing diuretic, but not a loop diuretic)
explanations: Incorrect. With documented severe (anaphylactic) sulfonamide reaction, exposing the patient to another sulfonamide-containing drug is risky.
Incorrect. Hydrochlorothiazide IS a sulfonamide and would be inappropriate.

Correct. Ethacrynic acid is the only commercially available non-sulfonamide loop diuretic. It is chemically distinct from the other loop diuretics (which all share a sulfonamide moiety) and from antibacterial sulfonamides. It is reserved for patients with documented severe sulfa allergy. Disadvantages: more ototoxic than other loop diuretics (especially with rapid IV administration), more GI side effects, and limited availability.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide IS a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and may cross-react.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is K+-sparing, not a loop diuretic — and is too weak for acute pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with HFrEF and CKD (eGFR 30) is on furosemide 240 mg daily but his urine output is decreasing and his weight is rising. The team suspects diuretic resistance. Which of the following best characterizes the mechanisms underlying diuretic resistance in this clinical setting?
choices: Pharmacokinetic only — poor oral absorption is the sole mechanism
Pharmacodynamic only — chronic NCC upregulation in the DCT is the only mechanism
Aldosterone-mediated only
Multifactorial: reduced delivery, distal NCC upregulation, RAAS, NSAIDs
Always due to patient nonadherence
explanations: Incorrect. Pharmacokinetics is one of several mechanisms, not the only one.
Incorrect. NCC upregulation is one of several mechanisms.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is one factor but not the sole cause.

Correct. Diuretic resistance has multiple coexisting causes: (1) reduced delivery to the TAL due to absorption issues, reduced GFR, reduced OAT-mediated proximal secretion (competing organic anions in CKD), and hypoalbuminemia (loop diuretics are highly protein-bound); (2) post-receptor 'braking' — chronic loop diuretic exposure upregulates NCC in the DCT and other distal Na+ reabsorption mechanisms, partially offsetting upstream blockade; (3) volume contraction reactivates RAAS, increasing distal Na+ retention; (4) NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated natriuresis and afferent vasodilation. Management: switch to IV, increase dose, add thiazide (sequential nephron blockade), restrict salt, treat underlying disease, address nonadherence/NSAID use.
Incorrect. While nonadherence can contribute, it is not the only cause; multiple physiologic mechanisms are operative.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with HFrEF and persistent edema on furosemide 240 mg/day is found to have diuretic resistance. Metolazone (a thiazide-like diuretic) is added as 'sequential nephron blockade.' Within 24 hours, he undergoes brisk diuresis. Compared with loop diuretic alone, which row best describes the effect of loop + thiazide combination on natriuresis and K+ wasting?
choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Correct. Sequential nephron blockade (loop + thiazide) addresses the 'braking phenomenon' of chronic loop monotherapy. With chronic loop diuretic alone, the upregulated NCC in the DCT increases distal Na+ reabsorption, partially offsetting the upstream NKCC2 blockade. Adding a thiazide blocks NCC, allowing more Na+ to reach the collecting duct. Distal Na+ delivery rises further, urinary Na+ output rises markedly, and K+ wasting also increases (more substrate for ENaC, more aldosterone activation). Combined diuresis is more effective but requires careful K+ monitoring; severe hypokalemia and contraction alkalosis are common with combination therapy. Often used short-term to break diuretic resistance.
Incorrect. Combination therapy increases (not decreases) all three.
Incorrect. Distal Na+ delivery up while urinary Na+ down is internally inconsistent.
Incorrect. Distal Na+ delivery is not reduced by adding thiazide; it is INCREASED (more Na+ flows past the DCT to the CD because NCC is blocked).
Incorrect. Combination therapy produces measurable changes in all three parameters.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome (serum albumin 1.8 g/dL, urine protein 8 g/day) and significant edema has poor response to oral furosemide. Which of the following best explains the diminished diuretic response in this patient?
choices: Mutations in NKCC2 caused by chronic glomerular disease
Hypoalbuminemia reduces tubular delivery of protein-bound furosemide
Increased renal blood flow shunts drug past the kidney
Decreased aldosterone production reduces principal cell ENaC activity
Direct ENaC inhibition by hypoalbuminemia
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 is not mutated by glomerular disease; the diuretic resistance is hemodynamic / pharmacokinetic.

Correct. Furosemide is ~95% protein-bound; the bound fraction is delivered to the tubular lumen via OAT-mediated proximal secretion (which extracts free drug from peritubular blood; bound drug serves as a reservoir). In hypoalbuminemia, total bound drug is lower and tubular delivery is reduced. Additionally, in nephrotic syndrome filtered albumin in urine binds intraluminal furosemide, sequestering it from the apical NKCC2 site. Strategies: (1) higher furosemide doses; (2) IV administration; (3) coadministration with albumin (theoretical merit; randomized trials show inconsistent benefit). Some experts also use thiazide for sequential nephron blockade.
Incorrect. RBF is not the principal issue; nephrotic patients often have normal RBF.
Incorrect. Aldosterone is typically ELEVATED in nephrotic syndrome (volume-contracted underfill), not decreased.
Incorrect. Hypoalbuminemia does not directly inhibit ENaC.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with HFrEF and CKD (eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73 m²) has poor response to furosemide 80 mg daily. Which of the following best explains why higher doses of loop diuretic are typically required in CKD?
choices: Loop diuretics should always be discontinued in CKD
Standard doses are more effective in CKD due to slower clearance
Higher doses needed due to reduced delivery and fewer nephrons
Loop diuretics are absolutely contraindicated in CKD
Loop diuretics should be replaced by thiazides in CKD (the opposite is true; thiazides are weaker in CKD)
explanations: Incorrect. Loop diuretics remain useful in CKD; they are not discontinued solely because of reduced GFR.
Incorrect. Standard doses are LESS effective in CKD because of reduced delivery to the tubule.

Correct. Loop diuretics in CKD: (1) reduced GFR limits filtered drug; (2) uremic organic anions compete with loop diuretic for proximal tubular OAT-mediated secretion, reducing tubular delivery; (3) fewer nephrons means fewer NKCC2 targets per gram of body. Doses up to 4-fold higher than usual (e.g., furosemide 200–400 mg/day, or even higher in severe CKD) are commonly required. Continuous IV infusion may be useful for high-volume patients. Because thiazides require functional nephrons for their effect AND adequate GFR for filtered delivery, they are LESS effective in advanced CKD — yet in some patients they retain enough effect to be useful in sequential nephron blockade.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics are first-line in CKD with volume overload; not contraindicated.
Incorrect. Thiazides are LESS effective in CKD; loop diuretics remain the preferred class for volume management.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF on furosemide develops worsening lower-extremity edema and reduced urine output after starting ibuprofen for knee pain 1 week ago. Which of the following best explains the impaired diuretic response in this patient?
choices: Ibuprofen directly inhibits NKCC2 in the TAL
Ibuprofen chemically chelates furosemide in the GI tract
Ibuprofen inhibits OAT-mediated proximal tubular secretion of furosemide, reducing tubular delivery to NKCC2
Ibuprofen activates aldosterone synthesis directly at the adrenal cortex
Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin-mediated natriuresis and afferent vasodilation
explanations: Incorrect. NSAIDs do not directly inhibit NKCC2.
Incorrect. NSAIDs do not chemically chelate furosemide.
Incorrect. While organic anion competition can occur, this is one mechanism among several; the question asks for the BEST explanation.
Incorrect. NSAIDs do not directly stimulate aldosterone; if anything, NSAIDs may reduce renin via prostaglandin inhibition.

Correct. NSAIDs blunt loop diuretic effect through multiple convergent mechanisms: (1) reduced PGE2/PGI2 contribution to natriuresis at the TAL; (2) afferent arteriolar constriction (loss of prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation), which lowers GFR and filtered drug delivery; (3) blunted IV venodilator effect; (4) competition with loop diuretic for OAT-mediated proximal secretion. Risk is greatest in volume-depleted patients (HF, cirrhosis), where afferent prostaglandin support is most needed. The 'triple whammy' of NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is a classic precipitant of AKI.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester with hypertensive emergency develops acute pulmonary edema. Which of the following best characterizes the use of furosemide in pregnancy?
choices: Furosemide is avoided in pregnancy unless clearly indicated
Loop diuretic is first-line for routine hypertension in pregnancy
Ethacrynic acid is the preferred loop diuretic in pregnancy
Loop diuretics are absolutely safe in pregnancy with no concerns
Furosemide is the antihypertensive of choice in preeclampsia
explanations: Correct. Furosemide crosses the placenta. Routine antihypertensive management in pregnancy uses methyldopa, labetalol, or nifedipine — not loop diuretics — to avoid potential reductions in uteroplacental perfusion from volume contraction. Furosemide IS used when the maternal indication is compelling, such as acute pulmonary edema or severe heart failure where the benefit clearly outweighs the risk to the fetus. Animal studies have shown some teratogenic effects at high doses; human data are limited, leading to FDA category C (now replaced by descriptive labeling). In late pregnancy and labor, furosemide is generally given with caution and electrolyte monitoring.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics are not first-line for routine pregnancy HTN.
Incorrect. Ethacrynic acid is reserved for sulfa-allergic patients; not routinely preferred in pregnancy.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics in pregnancy require risk-benefit consideration; they are not absolutely safe.
Incorrect. Hydralazine, labetalol, and nifedipine are preferred for severe hypertension in preeclampsia; loop diuretics are added only for pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man on chronic oral furosemide 80 mg daily is admitted with acute decompensated HF. The DOSE trial guides initial IV diuretic dosing in hospital. Which of the following best characterizes the standard initial IV dosing strategy in this setting?
choices: Halve the home oral dose for IV administration
Match the home oral dose 1:1 (assuming complete bioavailability)
Use only continuous IV infusion; bolus dosing is contraindicated
IV bolus at 1–2.5× the home oral dose daily
Always use spironolactone first instead of loop diuretic
explanations: Incorrect. Halving the dose under-doses; oral bioavailability of furosemide is only ~50%, so equivalent IV is HALF the oral dose, and acute decompensation often requires more than maintenance dosing.
Incorrect. Oral bioavailability of furosemide is ~50%, so 1:1 oral-to-IV underdoses; additionally, acute decompensation often requires escalation.
Incorrect. Both intermittent IV bolus AND continuous infusion are acceptable; the DOSE trial showed intermittent bolus is non-inferior.

Correct. The DOSE trial (NEJM 2011) compared low- vs high-dose IV furosemide and continuous vs intermittent dosing in acute decompensated HF. Initial IV dosing strategy: 2.5× the home daily oral dose given as IV bolus once or twice daily. (Adjusted for IV bioavailability, this approximates the home oral dose with some escalation.) High-dose strategy was associated with greater diuresis without significant adverse outcome differences. If response is inadequate after 2–6 hours, the dose can be doubled. Renal function, electrolytes, and weight are monitored closely.
Incorrect. Spironolactone has a slow onset and is too weak as monotherapy for acute decompensation; it is added later for chronic management.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with chronic salt craving, polyuria, and growth retardation is found to have hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypercalciuria, normal-low blood pressure, and elevated plasma renin and aldosterone. The pattern is similar to that seen in a patient on chronic furosemide. Which of the following best characterizes the underlying disorder?
choices: Gain-of-function mutation in ENaC (Liddle syndrome)
Loss-of-function NKCC2 mutation (Bartter syndrome)
Loss-of-function mutation in NCC (Gitelman syndrome) — but Gitelman has HYPOCALCIURIA, not hypercalciuria
Mineralocorticoid receptor mutation (PHA1) — would cause HYPERkalemia and salt wasting, with high aldosterone but resistance
AQP2 mutation (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) — would cause hypernatremia and dilute urine, not the hypokalemic alkalosis pattern
explanations: Incorrect. Liddle syndrome features HYPERtension, suppressed renin and aldosterone — opposite of this profile.

Correct. Bartter syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TAL transporters: NKCC2, ROMK, ClC-Kb, or barttin (which is essential for ClC-Kb function). The clinical biochemical pattern mirrors that of a patient on chronic high-dose furosemide: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypercalciuria with kidney stone risk, normal-low BP, elevated renin and aldosterone. Bartter is the 'natural phenocopy' of loop diuretic use. Gitelman is the analogous 'natural phenocopy' of thiazide use (NCC mutation), distinguished by HYPOCALCIURIA rather than hypercalciuria.
Incorrect. Gitelman would have HYPOCALCIURIA, not hypercalciuria; the hypercalciuria here points to a TAL lesion (Bartter), not DCT.
Incorrect. PHA1 features HYPERkalemia and metabolic acidosis with high aldosterone but mineralocorticoid resistance — opposite of this profile.
Incorrect. AQP2 mutation produces nephrogenic DI with dilute urine and hypernatremia, not hypokalemic alkalosis.
